problem: Existing navigation agents are task-specific (point, instruction, or object goal), rely on discretized action prediction that loses precision and adds latency, and struggle with long-horizon exploration and open-vocabulary understanding. Unified methods such as Uni-NaVid lack long-horizon planning, and MTU3D needs 3D object coordinate construction.
motivation: Real-world navigation needs low-latency control, long-horizon memory and exploration, and cross-task generalization in one system. The authors observe that navigation policies are learned easily, while failures mostly come from weak understanding of generic instructions and open-vocabulary objects. This motivates a fast-slow dual system trained jointly with generic vision-language data.
key_idea: A single Qwen2.5-VL-3B model with a fast flow-matching waypoint policy and a slow frontier/CoT subgoal planner, sharing a KV-cache memory and trained jointly on navigation plus general VL data, handles point, instruction and object goals plus exploration.
insight: Replacing autoregressive action chunks with a flow-matching waypoint head gives large gains: on OVON val-unseen SR goes from 35.3 to 43.5. The slow frontier system adds the largest gain on long-horizon OVON (43.5 to 55.9 SR), while general data (+1.8 SR) and CoT (+1.5 SR) add smaller stable gains. In the appendix, once the extra data is included, 3B and 7B models perform nearly the same (57.7 vs 57.9), so data diversity rather than model size is the bottleneck.
method: Unified multimodal tokenization: Qwen2.5-VL-3B with an added coordinate modality (MLP-embedded 2D coordinates and headings) plus text and ViT image tokens; a central memory keeps a ring buffer of pose-stamped images (up to 20 frames) with a KV cache for streaming.
Fast system: a DiT-style flow-matching policy head cross-attends to the VLM features and outputs H=5 waypoints (x, y, sinθ, cosθ, arrive flag) with 5 Euler steps, running at about 5 Hz.

Slow system: builds a 3D occupancy map to extract frontiers, links each frontier to a historical image (a visual proxy), and uses explicit chain-of-thought over the frontiers and memory to choose a subgoal or output the target location if it has been seen.
Fast-slow coordination: the slow system emits subgoal coordinates and subtasks, and the fast system executes them with continuous visual feedback (obstacle avoidance, final-pose adjustment).

Two-stage training: Stage 1 uses an autoregressive objective on discrete data (action chunks, QA, grounding, general data). Stage 2 attaches the flow-matching head and trains jointly with 20% of the Stage-1 discrete data to avoid degrading the VLM.
Data mix: CityWalker (point goal), R2R/RxR VLN-CE, HM3D OVON shortest paths, frontier-exploration trajectories, ScanQA and R2R-EnvDrop QA, MAmmoTH-VL general data, RefCOCO and Objects365 grounding.

setting.training_data: Navigation data from CityWalker, R2R/RxR VLN-CE, HM3D OVON, frontier-exploration trajectories, ScanQA and R2R-EnvDrop; plus general MAmmoTH-VL data, RefCOCO and Objects365 grounding, and a small amount of real-robot data. Stage 1 used 96 H20 GPUs for 120 h, Stage 2 used 64 H20 GPUs for 48 h.
setting.observation: Fast system: tri-view (front/left/right) monocular RGB with a 20-frame history. Slow system on OVON additionally uses depth and odometry to build the occupancy map.
setting.action_space: Predicted continuous waypoints (x, y, θ, arrive), 5 per step, executed by a speed controller
setting.simulator: Habitat (VLN-CE on Matterport3D, HM3D OVON) plus the CityWalker benchmark
setting.privileged: none (the slow system uses depth and odometry to build the occupancy map; no GT map)

numbers.extra: Panoramic RGB only, fast system only; jointly trained with general VL data

numbers_note: The point-goal result on the CityWalker benchmark is reported only as MAOE (11.53% vs CityWalker 15.23%), so it is not included in the numbers. Val-Seen-Synonyms for the fast-only OmniNav (SR 50.4, SPL 28.5) is also omitted. The table reports OS, which is recorded here as OSR.
results: With RGB only and the fast system alone, OmniNav reaches SR 69.5 on R2R-CE and 73.6 on RxR-CE val-unseen, beating CorrectNav (65.1 and 69.3). On HM3D-OVON val-unseen, the fast-only model gets SR 43.5, and adding the slow system with CoT gets SR 59.2 and SPL 33.2, versus MTU3D at SR 40.8.
limitations: The full slow system is not deployed on the real robot, because it needs LiDAR/depth integration. Real-world tests only use the fast system, and there is no latency analysis for the slow system.
The slow system depends on depth and odometry to build the occupancy map, so OVON results are not RGB-only, and frontier selection is heuristic.
Complex objects such as clothes, carpets and mirrors remain unstable, and the model-scale and data-scaling analysis is limited.
